    Huron · Implementation atlas

    Inside the Metastore

    Adapters, ports, and the constraints that turn catalog, governance, and credential records into durable PostgreSQL rows, with the in-memory references they are measured against.

    29 adapter declarationsPostgreSQL and memory adapters13 UML viewsOffline-ready

    Implementation snapshot: 16 September 2026, working tree based on e71e685. The editable Markdown source contains all Mermaid diagrams and responsibility notes.

    The metastore is Huron's relational persistence tier: one PostgreSQL adapter per capability, each holding an asyncpg pool it never closes, plus the in-memory reference stores the unit suites and contract scenarios run against. It implements the persistence ports that Catalog, Raw and Security declare, decodes rows into their canonical owner values, and translates the database constraints a request can legitimately hit into the same domain errors the in-memory stores raise. It holds no business rules of its own: visibility, uniqueness, optimistic concurrency, idempotency, and lease fencing are contracts it enforces in SQL or in dictionaries on behalf of callers that decide.

    This is one class model presented in focused views. It includes every class and protocol declared in src/huron/core/metastore/ (29 declarations across 17 Python files, including the four memory credential adapters and shared Security fact projections; no enums) together with decoders and query helpers that explain their structure. The ports these adapters conform to are shown as <<Protocol>> neighbors with their declared members; the records they return and the values they consume are <<External>> boxes without internals, since the catalog atlas documents them. Repeated boxes denote the same class. Long parameter lists are abbreviated. This is a Python class diagram, not a database ER diagram: table and constraint names appear only where an adapter depends on them by name.

    Currency matters: huron.core.metastore is a concrete adapter owner within Core. Its permitted Huron dependencies are Catalog, Raw, Security and Foundation; domains never import it. Application wiring creates/closes pools; migrations remain under migrations/. The core map follows the same working tree. This source inventory does not declare migration-wide gates complete.

    Reading the diagrams

    • A --> B: association/reference, including a held pool, connection, or buffer.
    • A ..> B: uses, creates, returns, or raises B; the label states which.
    • A *-- B: A constructs and owns B as part of its object structure.
    • A --|> B: actual Python inheritance, including the ingest mixin bases.
    • A ..|> B: structural conformance to a Python protocol, not inheritance.
    • <<Protocol>>, <<Frozen>>, <<External>>, <<Module>>, and <<Neighbor>> identify roles. A <<Module>> box lists a module's public functions.
    • Private names (_TransactionWriter, _Projection) are real declarations that the public stores construct; they are shown because they carry the structure.
    • "In-memory" classes are the reference implementations; "Postgres" classes are the production adapters. Both satisfy the same port and the same contract scenarios.

    1. The metastore at a glance

    The six PostgreSQL API-facing adapters share one pool that the application lifespan opens. The two maintenance adapters take a separately authenticated cutover pool from the lakectl wiring and are never constructed by the API. Ports on the left half belong to Raw (HierarchyStore), Security (RbacStore, ApiKeyWriter and credential stores), and Integrity (DatabaseExclusion, LegacyMaintenance). Conformance is structural; Metastore can import owner values and permitted ports but never Integrity.

    Responsibility Owner Important contract
    Decode rows rows module One function per SELECT shape; total over the named columns; no I/O, validation, or error mapping. jsonb and array columns become mappings and frozensets here.
    Discover the hierarchy _PostgresCollection, _MemoryCollection Visibility is evaluated before LIMIT; hidden and absent both raise ResourceNotFound; keyset cursor is (slug, id) in C collation.
    Write the hierarchy atomically _PostgresTransactionWriter, _TransactionWriter One connection-held transaction or one buffered, lock-serialized block; slug/tag uniqueness and version CAS are translated to SlugExists, TagExists, PreconditionFailed.
    Guarantee exactly-once writes The transaction writers' claim/remember (principal, key) rows with a 24-hour TTL; an unfinished ingest_commit replay never expires; a different request digest is IdempotencyKeyReused.
    Keep the ingest ledger Ingest reader/writer mixins Session and file edges are fenced on etag, state, and recorded parts; leases only move forward; the sweep's expiry is fenced on the lapsed lease.
    Store governance PostgresRbacStore, InMemoryRbacStore Grants are validated with compile_binding before any write; service accounts insert their principal in the same transaction; policies preserve spec verbatim.
    Store credentials Four PostgreSQL and four memory adapters in Metastore Rows keep only digests and timestamps; expiry and revocation are judged by Security.
    Project authoritative facts SecurityFacts plus hierarchy readers Narrow Security-owned ancestry and organization-name projections reuse visibility-filtered Catalog readers.
    Fence and cut over PostgresRoleExclusion, PostgresLegacyMaintenance Operator-only; verifies the database identity, revokes dedicated application roles, and imports verified legacy inventory under schema 0010_independent_raw.

    2. Row decoders and typed projections

    Sources: rows.py, queries.py.

    rows is the single asyncpg boundary. Each decoder names exactly the columns one store's SELECT aliases; project renames classification_default to data_classification, release reads revision_number from a joined dataset_revisions row, api_key_record renames owner_subject and stringifies project_id, and dataset deliberately ignores the row's own data_classification column because no port reads it back. affected_row_count parses the command tag an execute() returns, which is how bulk revokes and CAS updates learn whether they touched a row.

    Each _Projection is a trusted SELECT whose WHERE clause takes the same four visibility parameters: unrestricted flag, organization ids, project ids, dataset ids. An organization is visible when named directly or when it owns a visible project or dataset; a project when named directly or when it owns a visible dataset; a dataset when its project or itself is named. _PostgresCollection.get wraps the projection as a subquery and adds WHERE id = $5; browse adds the parent filter and the (slug COLLATE "C", id) keyset cursor and fetches limit + 1 rows.

    3. The in-memory hierarchy reference

    Sources: hierarchy.py, Security fact projection mixin.

    InMemoryHierarchyStore is the reference every backend is compared against. Its transaction() takes one asyncio.Lock for the whole block, hands out a _TransactionWriter that stages into a fresh TransactionBuffer, and applies the buffer to the live dictionaries in one await-free step only if the block exits without raising. Reads never take the lock. Because the lock covers the entire transaction, no second transaction can observe a claim whose remember has not yet run, so claim needs no extra check for that case.

    The staged writers check uniqueness against both the live dictionaries and the buffer, so two inserts of one slug in one transaction conflict just as they would across transactions. insert_dataset accepts data_classification for parity with Postgres and discards it. latest_committed_revision assumes every held revision is committed, which is true because the in-memory writer never records another state. _MemoryCollection sorts visible children by (slug, id) and bisects on the cursor; _window and _trim_window produce the same limit + 1 semantics in memory and over a fetched page respectively.

    4. The PostgreSQL hierarchy adapter

    Sources: hierarchy.py, queries.py.

    transaction() acquires one connection and opens a transaction on it; every statement the yielded writer runs is issued on that connection, and nothing it writes is visible elsewhere until the block commits. Reads acquire from the pool directly and never see a partial transaction.

    Constraint translation. The insert methods catch UniqueViolationError and ForeignKeyViolationError and compare constraint_name against names fixed at module level: organizations_slug_key, projects_organization_id_slug_key, datasets_project_id_slug_key, releases_dataset_id_tag_key, and the composite releases_revision_dataset_fk. A matching name becomes SlugExists, TagExists, or ResourceNotFound; any other violation is re-raised untranslated. _PostgresDescriptionWriter.describe runs a single UPDATE ... WHERE id AND version = expected RETURNING id, and a missing row is PreconditionFailed.

    Idempotency. claim stakes an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (principal, key) DO UPDATE whose WHERE only takes over a row that has expired and is not an ingest_commit replay. Winning returns None. Losing reads the live row FOR UPDATE, raises IdempotencyKeyReused on a different digest, and otherwise returns the remembered Replay. remember stores {"kind", "id"} as jsonb with status 201. The 24-hour TTL is an SQL interval literal here and the _CLAIM_TTL constant in memory; the two are not bound together.

    5. Ingest-ledger mixins

    Sources: ingest.py.

    This module is a size split, not a port: the four mixins supply the ingest half of the write and read surfaces that hierarchy.py's concrete classes inherit. The mixins declare the attributes they expect (_store, _buffer, _connection, _clock, _pool, _sessions, _files) as annotations only; the host class sets them. ingest.py imports hierarchy.py's classes solely under TYPE_CHECKING, so the mutual import forms no runtime cycle.

    _reserve_ingest_session is shared by both writers so a reservation always has fresh uuid7 ids, etag 1, PREPARING, and a lease of exactly LEASE_TTL. begin_ingest refuses a missing dataset with ResourceNotFound and an open session with DatasetLocked carrying the blocking session's id, state, and expiry. In Postgres the one_open_ingest_per_dataset partial unique index is a backstop that also maps to DatasetLocked. freeze_commit returns an existing frozen intent for an identical retry while the session is COMMITTING or COMMITTED, and otherwise requires VERIFYING at the expected etag. Every other edge is one guarded UPDATE whose zero-row result is PreconditionFailed, except renew_ingest_session, which uses GREATEST so a lease never moves backward and raises IngestSessionExpired for a terminal or RECOVERING session.

    6. Port conformance of the hierarchy classes

    Sources: Raw ports, Catalog ports, Security facts, Foundation retry, hierarchy adapter, fact implementation, application conformance.

    Both stores satisfy separate Raw, Catalog and Security contracts; Raw's HierarchyStore no longer inherits release or Security facts, and its writer extends only Foundation's retry contract. The concrete transaction writer still implements all atomic groups on the same acquired connection or memory buffer. Application capabilities.py composes the ports and checks structural conformance.

    SecurityFacts.resource_scope uses the existing reader predicates: target discovery precedes scope construction, and dataset ancestry reads its parent only after target admission. organization_slug serves already-authorized account provisioning. Project classifications and dataset parents remain on the concrete hierarchy readers. These projections avoid a Security → Catalog dependency. See the shared Security fact contract and hierarchy contract.

    7. Governance persistence

    Sources: Metastore RBAC, Security ports, Security facts, Security governance values.

    Both stores run compile_binding on every grant before checking for duplicates or touching a table, so an unknown role, a service-account principal, or an unbindable scope raises the matching RoleError subclass first. The in-memory store keeps the compiled bindings keyed by binding id and answers bindings_for by lookup. The Postgres store joins role_bindings to role_capabilities, filters expiry against the database's now(), and rebuilds one control-capability Binding plus one per-layer Binding for each data.read/data.write row, so a DENY effect written outside the API is reproduced faithfully. The role_bindings_guard and service_accounts_kind_guard triggers exist for rows written outside this store; in the request path they never fire.

    Divergences worth knowing. PostgresRbacStore.create_service_account inserts the principals row and the service_accounts row in one transaction and maps the principals_subject_key violation to UsernameTaken; the in-memory store keeps no principal rows and cannot raise that error. In-memory disable_service_account mutates the stored ServiceAccount in place (the record is not frozen), while Postgres updates principals.disabled_at only for kind = 'service_account' and re-reads. attach_policy in Postgres can raise ScopeNotBindable, a RoleError, when the CHECK refuses SYSTEM; create_policy can raise a bare ValueError on the policy_type CHECK. Both are unreachable through the API's validated routes. The in-memory store serializes writes with a threading.RLock, not an asyncio lock, and its bindings_for returns expired grants too, leaving expiry to decide(), whereas the Postgres query drops rows expired at database now(). Ordering uses COLLATE "C" in SQL and plain sorted() in memory so keyset cursors agree byte for byte.

    8. Credential and principal stores

    Sources: PostgreSQL API keys, credentials, principals, sessions, memory API keys, memory credentials, memory principals, memory sessions, Security ports, API-key mechanism, password mechanism, principal contract, session mechanism.

    These four adapters are one statement per method against a primary key or a partial index, and they judge nothing: revoked keys, expired sessions, and disabled principals are returned as stored for ApiKeyResolver, SessionResolver, and the Security login workflows to refuse. Their memory counterparts live in this package, with no adapter re-exports through Security. ApiKeyStore and its ApiKeyWriter extension both belong to Security.

    • PostgresApiKeyStore.add maps a foreign-key refusal to ResourceNotFound and a key_id collision to RuntimeError, since a 128-bit random handle colliding is a bug, not a client error. revoke_all_for touches only rows whose revoked_at is still NULL and reports the count from the command tag.
    • PostgresCredentialStore.upsert is one INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE. The local_credentials_kind_guard trigger raises the same message for an unknown principal and a service account, so the store repeats the lookup to choose between ResourceNotFound and PrincipalKindMismatch.
    • PostgresPrincipalStore.upsert_oidc_user conflicts on idp_subject alone and only refreshes display_name; a first-ever idp_subject that collides with another principal's subject is refused as PrincipalSubjectExists, never auto-linked. get_user_by_subject folds unknown, disabled, and service-account subjects into one None so password verification keeps a constant shape.
    • PostgresSessionStore.touch relies on the caller clamping idle_expires_at to the absolute expiry that the table's CHECK enforces.

    9. Maintenance and legacy cutover

    Sources: maintenance.py, legacy.py, integrity/ports.py.

    These two adapters serve the operator-only core/integrity cutover, which the catalog atlas leaves outside its scope. DatabaseFence is a protocol declared here that Integrity's FenceEvidence document satisfies structurally, so the adapter never imports Integrity. Application wiring supplies PostgresRoleExclusion to the public ControllerAdmission workflow through an async context factory and retains pool lifetime ownership.

    PostgresRoleExclusion.identify reports the primary's system_identifier/oid/datname and refuses a replica. exclude verifies that identity against the fence, requires every role to be dedicated (no superuser, createdb, createrole, replication, or bypass-RLS attribute; not the session user; owning no objects), sets NOLOGIN, revokes the legacy roles' memberships and schema privileges, terminates their backends, and then runs check. check fails if any fenced role can log in, has a live session, or retains effective write, create, or security-definer access. Every failure is a ValueError; the adapter refuses owner-role deployments rather than transferring objects.

    PostgresLegacyMaintenance requires alembic_version to be exactly 0010_independent_raw on every call. lookup requires the full slug-and-id ancestry to match before trusting a revision identity and refuses colliding identities. resolve runs one transaction that locks open ingest sessions, imports each verified revision idempotently (ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING, then re-reads and compares), marks revisions with findings DEGRADED, records reconciliation_findings and integrity.cutover audit rows keyed by uuid5(run_id, ...), and terminalizes each session as COMMITTED only when it was COMMITTING against a finding-free verified final, otherwise FAILED.

    10. Values, clocks, and shared conventions

    Sources: Catalog Window and PlatformRoot, Foundation retry values, Raw LedgerEntry, Foundation Clock, Security visibility, Metastore exports.

    None of these values is declared in Metastore except SystemClock in hierarchy.py. Consumers import Window/PlatformRoot from Catalog, IdempotencyClaim/Replay and Clock from Foundation, LedgerEntry/AuditEvent from Raw, and Visibility from Security. The adapter package no longer re-exports those domain values; its four fields are exactly the four SQL parameters every projection binds.

    Convention In memory PostgreSQL
    Transaction One asyncio.Lock for the block; buffer applied on clean exit. One acquired connection with connection.transaction().
    Uniqueness Scan live plus staged records. Named UNIQUE constraints translated by constraint_name.
    Version CAS Compare version against the live record. UPDATE ... WHERE version = $expected RETURNING id.
    Ingest fencing Compare etag, state, lease, and parts in Python. Guarded UPDATE; zero affected rows is a conflict.
    Idempotency TTL _CLAIM_TTL of 24 hours from the injected clock. interval '24 hours' in SQL from the injected clock.
    Time Clock.now() for claims and leases; datetime.now(UTC) in RBAC. Same, plus database now() for binding expiry and key/session stamps.
    Cursor order sorted() on (slug, id), (tag,), (name, id). ORDER BY ... COLLATE "C" to match byte order.

    11. Application construction

    Sources: app.py, runtime.py, lakectl/wiring.py.

    The API lifespan calls asyncpg.create_pool(settings.database_url), constructs the six adapters over that pool with one SystemClock, bundles them as ApiStores, and closes the pool on shutdown. When a caller injects ApiStores no pool is opened; the test suites inject the in-memory hierarchy and RBAC stores and the Metastore memory credential stores that way. lakectl opens its own pool with maintenance credentials and constructs the cutover adapters. Alembic migrations live in migrations/; applications own pool construction and lifetime.

    12. Errors the adapters raise

    Sources: Foundation errors, Catalog errors, Raw errors, Security errors, Security roles, Security principals.

    Raised by Error Trigger
    Collections, reads ResourceNotFound Absent or hidden entity, release, revision, session, file, binding, account, policy; a foreign key refusing a parent.
    Description writers, ingest edges PreconditionFailed Version or etag mismatch; a fenced state, lease, or recorded-parts check failing.
    Transaction claim IdempotencyKeyReused Live claim with a different request digest.
    Hierarchy inserts SlugExists, TagExists Named UNIQUE constraint or live-plus-staged scan.
    begin_ingest DatasetLocked Open session for the dataset, or the partial unique index.
    renew_ingest_session IngestSessionExpired Terminal or RECOVERING session.
    RBAC store BindingExists, ServiceAccountExists, AttachmentExists, UsernameTaken Duplicate grant, name, attachment, or subject.
    RBAC store RoleError subclasses from compile_binding; ScopeNotBindable from the attachment CHECK Invalid grant; SYSTEM attachment.
    Credential and principal stores PrincipalKindMismatch, PrincipalSubjectExists Password on a service account; subject already held.
    Maintenance, legacy, policy CHECK, key collision ValueError, RuntimeError Not domain errors: operator-facing refusals and unreachable-by-design failures.

    DomainError carries status codes and problem data for the API's exception handlers. The maintenance adapters deliberately raise plain ValueError, since they are driven by lakectl, not by HTTP requests.

    Source and behavioral cross-checks

    The implementation snapshot was traced through constructors, fields, inheritance, protocol declarations, SQL statements, and constraint names. Useful behavioral entry points are:

    • Hierarchy contract scenarios run by the in-memory suite and the Postgres contract suite: atomicity, uniqueness, optimistic concurrency, idempotency, revision resolution, ordering, windowing, and the three visibility rules.
    • Catalog store contracts, RBAC store contracts, and auth store contracts: adapter behavior against a migrated database.
    • Row decoder tests and port value tests: decoding and the package's public surface.
    • Postgres RBAC conflicts, API-key conflicts, and credential conflicts: constraint-name translation with a faked pool.
    • Repository hierarchy tests and repository RBAC tests: core workflows driven over the in-memory stores.
    • Maintenance adapter tests, legacy verification tests, maintenance ownership contracts, and integrity store contracts: role fencing and cutover import.

    This document describes inspected implementation; it does not claim that the application test suites were rerun to create a diagram.
